riskReasons: RHS accepts the hyphenated name, while institutional and commercial records also use ‘Higasa yama’ and ‘Higasayama’.
The cultivar's spring variegation and leaf shape can change markedly through the season, creating visual and descriptive inconsistency.
Credible sources support a distinct variegated Acer palmatum, but the lean review does not resolve every historical near-name or older synonym claim.

duplicateCheck.notes: Compared with RC-007 ‘Butterfly’ and other variegated maples. RHS accepted usage, a dated RHS specimen and two living collections support a distinct cultivar identity. ‘Higasa yama’ and ‘Higasayama’ are orthographic variants; unverified historical names are not promoted to synonyms. C0 resolves as unique with targeted spelling review complete.

identityNotes: The Atlas uses the RHS accepted hyphenated form ‘Higasa-yama’. The spaced form used by JC Raulston and Dawes and the joined herbarium-label form ‘Higasayama’ resolve to the same stable identity. Potential near-names and historical labels require separate evidence and are not adopted as synonyms in this lean profile.

content.summary: An upright variegated Japanese maple whose crinkled seven-lobed leaves open with cream, pink and green tones, become greener as the season advances and finish in mixed orange, yellow and red.
content.habit: Vigorous upright deciduous shrub or small tree, developing a broad crown with age. Living-collection records support a medium to larger garden specimen rather than a permanent dwarf.
content.leafForm: Palmate leaves commonly described with seven slender, pointed, toothed and crinkled lobes. Spring variegation combines cream, pink and green, but the pattern can fade or change as leaves mature.

seasonal.spring: New leaves unfurl tightly and display the strongest cream-to-pink variegation with green structure; timing and intensity vary.
seasonal.summer: Foliage becomes greener, often retaining cream or pale vein and margin effects; some shoots may appear less variegated.
seasonal.autumn: Leaves may turn orange, dark yellow and red; the mix is variable and should not be represented as a fixed palette.

size.qualifier: JC Raulston lists 15–20 ft and measured one accession at 12 ft in 2023; Dawes describes about 20 ft high and wide. Treat these as mature living-collection contexts, not a universal maximum.

content.cultivation: Grow in moist but well-drained soil in sun to partial shade, with shelter from drying exposure. Variegated spring foliage benefits from protection from intense heat and unreliable moisture.
content.diagnostic: Compare with RC-007 ‘Butterfly’: both are variegated Acer palmatum, but ‘Higasa-yama’ is characterised by crinkled, many-toned spring leaves and an upright larger framework, rather than ‘Butterfly’s’ irregular pale margins. Variegation alone does not authenticate either cultivar.
content.confidence: High confidence in the accepted cultivar identity, Acer palmatum placement and broad variegated seasonal character. Moderate confidence in stable year-to-year patterning, exact mature size and historical synonymy.
content.unresolvedIssue: Seasonal variegation may be weak, altered or partly green on some growth. The lean review does not resolve all historical names sometimes associated with the cultivar, so only the spelling variants are governed.
